lessons.title: Differentiate response-masked Direct Preference Optimization
lessons.body:
# Differentiate response-masked Direct Preference Optimization

DPO compares the policy’s chosen-versus-rejected log-probability margin with a frozen reference margin. Summing only response targets keeps prompt and padding positions out of that comparison. Length normalization would change the objective, rather than merely improve numerical stability. Softplus evaluates the binary preference likelihood without explicitly taking a logarithm of a near-zero sigmoid. Reference ownership is observable in autograd: an accidental gradient into the reference changes the optimization problem even when the scalar loss initially looks correct.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F
margin = torch.tensor([-1000., 0., 1000.])
print(F.softplus(-margin))
```

## Review the evidence

Audit pair identity, response masks, length bias and preference provenance. A decreasing preference loss does not by itself establish helpfulness, safety or generalization to new prompt groups.
lessons.task: Inputs are finite floating [batch,2,time,vocab] logits and int64 [batch,2,time] aligned response targets; pair index 0 is chosen, 1 rejected, and -100 masks non-response positions. Sum valid token log probabilities for each response, not their length average. Return mean(softplus(-beta*((policy_chosen-policy_rejected)-(reference_chosen-reference_rejected)))). Detach all reference logits. Every response needs a valid target. Reject bad labels, shape, empty batches and nonpositive/nonfinite beta. This is the DPO objective, not a claim of aligned behavior from passing a small fixture.

lessons.solution:
import math
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

def dpo_loss(policy, reference, targets, beta=.1):
    if policy.ndim!=4 or policy.shape[1]!=2 or min(policy.shape)==0 or policy.shape[-1]<2 or reference.shape!=policy.shape or targets.shape!=policy.shape[:-1]:raise ValueError('Expected [batch, pair=2, time, vocabulary] aligned logits and targets.')
    if not policy.is_floating_point() or not reference.is_floating_point() or targets.dtype!=torch.long or not torch.isfinite(policy).all() or not torch.isfinite(reference).all() or not math.isfinite(beta) or beta<=0:raise ValueError('Expected finite floating logits, int64 labels and beta > 0.')
    mask=targets!=-100
    if (mask.sum(-1)==0).any() or ((targets[mask]<0)|(targets[mask]>=policy.shape[-1])).any():raise ValueError('Every response needs valid in-vocabulary targets.')
    safe=targets.masked_fill(~mask,0)
    policy_sum=(policy.log_softmax(-1).gather(-1,safe.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)*mask).sum(-1)
    reference_sum=(reference.detach().log_softmax(-1).gather(-1,safe.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)*mask).sum(-1)
    margin=(policy_sum[:,0]-policy_sum[:,1])-(reference_sum[:,0]-reference_sum[:,1])
    result=F.softplus(-beta*margin).mean()
    return result

lessons.title: Own grouped advantages and the clipped policy surrogate
lessons.body:
# Own grouped advantages and the clipped policy surrogate

Grouped policy optimization compares completions of the same prompt rather than fitting a value baseline. Reward normalization must use that prompt’s group, and old policy scores are immutable evidence from rollout collection. Clipping limits the surrogate incentive after a ratio crosses a boundary, with different signs for good and bad advantages. Per-response token reduction prevents long completions from acquiring accidental extra weight. The Lab deliberately separates this mechanism from an end-to-end RL training system.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
rewards = torch.tensor([[1., 3., 2.]])
a = rewards - rewards.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
print(a / (rewards.std(-1, correction=0, keepdim=True)+1e-8))
```

## Review the evidence

Inspect constant-reward groups, stale rollout policies and response masks. Normalizing rewards is not a substitute for an informative reward function, a reference policy or an evaluation protocol.
lessons.task: Implement the GRPO-style clipped surrogate core for [prompts,completions,tokens] sampled log probabilities. Use detached within-prompt reward advantages normalized by population standard deviation plus 1e-8. Compute exp(logp-old_logp.detach()), take the minimum of unclipped and [1-clip,1+clip] clipped ratio times advantage, average over valid tokens within each response, then equally over prompts/completions. Detach rewards. Require each response to contain a token, at least two completions, 0<clip<1 and absolute log-ratio<=20. This exercise isolates the surrogate; rollout collection, a reference-KL penalty and reward design are separate components.

lessons.title: Handle multiple positives and singleton anchors in SupCon
lessons.body:
# Handle multiple positives and singleton anchors in SupCon

Pairwise contrastive learning assigns one positive per observation; supervised contrastive learning can assign several. Averaging individual positive log probabilities differs from taking the logarithm of their summed probability. A singleton label has no positive anchor loss but can still be a useful negative for another class. Removing its entire row and column would change the objective. Masked numerical operations also matter: multiplying an invalid diagonal by zero can still propagate NaNs.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
labels = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1])
same = labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]
print(same & ~torch.eye(3,dtype=torch.bool))
```

## Review the evidence

Review positive identity and augmentation policy separately from class labels. Test invariance to joint permutation and positive scaling, then assess representation quality on a genuinely held-out downstream task.
lessons.task: Normalize finite nonzero [N,D] embeddings, exclude self pairs from every softmax denominator, and average log probability over all same-label non-self positives for each anchor. Average only anchors that have a positive; singleton embeddings still appear as negatives for other anchors. Require N>=2, aligned int64 labels, temperature>0, and at least one positive pair. Preserve gradients to every participating embedding. Avoid zero times negative infinity on masked diagonals.
lessons.starter:
import math
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

def supervised_contrastive(embeddings, labels, temperature=.1):
    # TODO: implement supervised_contrastive under the declared contract.
    return None
lessons.solution:
import math
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

def supervised_contrastive(embeddings, labels, temperature=.1):
    if embeddings.ndim!=2 or len(embeddings)<2 or embeddings.shape[1]==0 or labels.shape!=(len(embeddings),) or labels.dtype!=torch.long:raise ValueError('Expected [N>=2,D] embeddings and aligned int64 labels.')
    if not embeddings.is_floating_point() or not torch.isfinite(embeddings).all() or (embeddings.norm(dim=1)==0).any() or not math.isfinite(temperature) or temperature<=0:raise ValueError('Embeddings must be finite and nonzero; temperature must be positive.')
    diagonal=torch.eye(len(embeddings),dtype=torch.bool,device=embeddings.device)
    positive=(labels[:,None]==labels[None,:])&~diagonal
    counts=positive.sum(-1)
    valid=counts>0
    if not valid.any():raise ValueError('At least one non-self positive pair is required.')
    z=F.normalize(embeddings,dim=-1)
    scores=(z@z.T/temperature).masked_fill(diagonal,float('-inf'))
    log_prob=scores-torch.logsumexp(scores,-1,keepdim=True)
    selected=torch.where(positive,log_prob,torch.zeros_like(log_prob))
    per_anchor=-selected.sum(-1)/counts.clamp_min(1)
    return per_anchor[valid].mean()

import math
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.9, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float64)

lessons.title: Route sparse top-two experts with an explicit capacity policy
lessons.body:
# Route sparse top-two experts with an explicit capacity policy

A sparse router introduces a discrete ownership decision between differentiable computations. The selected gate probabilities remain trainable, but selection indices and capacity decisions do not. Overflow policy changes which examples reach which expert; this exercise makes input-order admission and renormalization explicit. Load balancing uses pre-capacity assignments so dropping work cannot masquerade as balanced demand. CPU execution demonstrates correctness and gradients, not expert-parallel communication, a distributed all-to-all operation or an inference speedup.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
p = torch.tensor([[.2, .6, .2]])
print(p.argsort(descending=True, stable=True))
```

## Review the evidence

Inspect requested versus accepted loads, dropped work and gate gradients. Define a production overflow policy and measure expert utilization before choosing a capacity factor or claiming sparse efficiency.
lessons.task: For finite floating [tokens,dim] x, a Linear router with E>=2 outputs and E Linear experts of one common output width, choose the two largest router softmax probabilities per token (ties by expert index). Process tokens in input order; accept an assignment while that expert has capacity. Renormalize the retained gates per token. A token whose two assignments overflow returns graph-connected zeros. Return (output, auxiliary, accepted_loads, dropped_assignments). Auxiliary is E*sum(mean_full_router_probability*detached_pre_capacity_top2_fraction), fractions normalized by 2*tokens. Execute only accepted expert rows; do not evaluate every expert densely. Reject invalid shapes, nonfinite inputs/parameters and nonpositive integer capacity.
lessons.starter:
import torch

def sparse_mixture(x, router, experts, capacity):
    # TODO: implement sparse_mixture under the declared contract.
    return None
lessons.solution:
import torch

def sparse_mixture(x, router, experts, capacity):
    if x.ndim!=2 or min(x.shape)==0 or not x.is_floating_point() or not torch.isfinite(x).all() or type(capacity)!=int or capacity<=0:raise ValueError('Expected finite nonempty token matrix and positive integer capacity.')
    count=len(experts)
    if count<2 or not isinstance(router,torch.nn.Linear) or router.in_features!=x.shape[1] or router.out_features!=count:raise ValueError('Router and expert count must match.')
    if any(not isinstance(e,torch.nn.Linear) or e.in_features!=x.shape[1] or e.out_features!=experts[0].out_features for e in experts):raise ValueError('Experts must share input/output dimensions.')
    if any(not torch.isfinite(p).all() for m in [router,*experts] for p in m.parameters()):raise ValueError('Model parameters must be finite.')
    probabilities=router(x).softmax(-1)
    chosen=probabilities.argsort(dim=-1,descending=True,stable=True)[:,:2]
    requested=torch.bincount(chosen.flatten(),minlength=count).to(x.dtype)/(2*len(x))
    auxiliary=count*(probabilities.mean(0)*requested.detach()).sum()
    accepted=torch.zeros_like(probabilities,dtype=torch.bool)
    loads=[]
    for expert in range(count):
        tokens=(chosen==expert).any(-1).nonzero().flatten()[:capacity]
        accepted[tokens,expert]=True
        loads.append(len(tokens))
    retained=probabilities*accepted
    gates=retained/retained.sum(-1,keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-12)
    zero=(x.sum()+probabilities.sum())*0
    output=x.new_zeros((len(x),experts[0].out_features))+zero
    for expert in range(count):
        tokens=accepted[:,expert].nonzero().flatten()
        if len(tokens):
            contribution=experts[expert](x.index_select(0,tokens))*gates[tokens,expert,None]
            output=output.index_add(0,tokens,contribution)
    dropped=2*len(x)-sum(loads)
    return output,auxiliary,loads,dropped

checks.name: stable ties capacity and zero-output overflow
checks.code:
router = torch.nn.Linear(1, 3, bias=False)
experts = torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False) for _ in range(3)])
with torch.no_grad():
    router.weight.zero_()
    for i, e in enumerate(experts):
        e.weight.fill_(i + 1)
y, a, loads, dropped = sparse_mixture(torch.ones(3, 1), router, experts, 1)
assert loads == [1, 1, 0] and dropped == 4 and torch.allclose(y, torch.tensor([[1.5], [0.0], [0.0]])) and (abs(a.item() - 1) < 1e-06), 'Contract failed: stable ties capacity and zero-output overflow.'

lessons.title: Preserve target mass with speculative accept and residual resampling
lessons.body:
# Preserve target mass with speculative accept and residual resampling

A draft model proposes cheaply, but naive verification would change the target distribution. Speculative sampling accepts some draft mass and compensates on rejection using the positive residual between target and draft probabilities. That residual is not simply the target distribution again. Making both uniform draws explicit separates the probability transform from RNG ownership and permits deterministic boundary tests. The Lab studies one categorical verification step, not a multi-token cached transformer execution pipeline.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
p = torch.tensor([.2, .8])
q = torch.tensor([.8, .2])
print((p-q).clamp_min(0))
```

## Review the evidence

Check support mismatch, equal distributions and rejection boundaries. Correct target mass is necessary for speculative generation, while speed depends on model costs, acceptance rates and the actual hardware pipeline.
lessons.task: Implement one exact categorical speculative step for normalized finite nonnegative [vocab] probabilities. The proposed token must have positive draft mass. Accept it when accept_uniform < min(1,target[proposal]/draft[proposal]). On rejection, inverse-CDF sample from normalized clamp(target-draft,min=0), using residual_uniform and right-open CDF bins. Return (token, accepted). Uniforms are explicit finite values in [0,1), so the function owns no RNG. Reject invalid probabilities, token indices and uniforms. This single-position probability mechanism makes no wall-clock speed claim.

lessons.title: Search a finite-state grammar with explicit EOS and sequence scores
lessons.body:
# Search a finite-state grammar with explicit EOS and sequence scores

A grammar constrains valid sequences, while a language model supplies their scores. Filtering illegal transitions after normalizing the original vocabulary preserves the declared model likelihood; renormalizing only legal tokens instead creates a different conditional distribution. Finished EOS paths need their own lifetime, otherwise they can be accidentally extended or charged extra probability. This finite-position exercise makes search and grammar correctness inspectable without a remote model. A narrow beam can still prune the best complete sequence.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
scores = torch.tensor([[2., 0., -1.]])
print(scores.log_softmax(-1))
```

## Review the evidence

Compare a wide beam with a brute-force oracle on short sequences. Define termination, tie breaking and length scoring before adding history-dependent model calls or claiming that beam search finds the global optimum.
lessons.task: Search finite floating [time,vocab] position-conditioned logits under transitions[state][token]=next_state. EOS is permitted only in accepting states and terminates the hypothesis without a transition. Use original full-vocabulary log-softmax scores before grammar filtering: do not renormalize each allowed subset. Keep finished hypotheses without scoring further tokens, sort by descending accumulated score then lexicographic token sequence, and retain width hypotheses after each step. Return {tokens,score} for the best finished hypothesis; reject if none finishes. Wide beams can match exhaustive search; a finite narrow beam is not guaranteed optimal.

checks.name: wide beam matches exhaustive allowed complete sequences
checks.code:
import itertools
x = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, -2.0], [1.0, 2.0, -1.0], [0.0, 0.0, 3.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
tr = {0: {0: 1, 1: 1}, 1: {0: 1, 1: 1}}
scores = x.log_softmax(-1)
candidates = []
for length in (2, 3):
    for prefix in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=length - 1):
        tokens = prefix + (2,)
        score = sum((scores[i, t].item() for i, t in enumerate(tokens)))
        candidates.append((tokens, score))
best = sorted(candidates, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))[0]
r = constrained_beam(x, tr, 0, {1}, 2, 20)
assert tuple(r['tokens']) == best[0] and abs(r['score'] - best[1]) < 1e-12, 'Contract failed: wide beam matches exhaustive allowed complete sequences.'

checks.name: EOS cannot terminate a nonaccepting prefix
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[0.0, 0.0, 10.0], [0.0, 0.0, 10.0]])
r = constrained_beam(x, {0: {0: 1}, 1: {}}, 0, {1}, 2, 4)
assert r['tokens'] == [0, 2], 'Contract failed: EOS cannot terminate a nonaccepting prefix.'

checks.name: finished paths retain their score and deterministic ties
checks.code:
x = torch.zeros(3, 3)
r = constrained_beam(x, {0: {0: 1, 1: 1}, 1: {0: 1, 1: 1}}, 0, {1}, 2, 8)
assert r['tokens'] == [0, 2] and abs(r['score'] - 2 * x.log_softmax(-1)[0, 0].item()) < 1e-06, 'Contract failed: finished paths retain their score and deterministic ties.'

checks.name: original full-vocabulary likelihood is retained
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[0.0, 9.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, 9.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
r = constrained_beam(x, {0: {0: 1}, 1: {}}, 0, {1}, 2, 4)
expected = x.log_softmax(-1)[0, 0] + x.log_softmax(-1)[1, 2]
assert abs(r['score'] - expected.item()) < 1e-12 and r['score'] < -8, 'Contract failed: original full-vocabulary likelihood is retained.'

lessons.title: Project: train and reload a local DPO policy with LoRA ownership
lessons.body:
# Project: train and reload a local DPO policy with LoRA ownership

Preference optimization needs more evidence than a scalar loss formula. This project owns a local supervised base, a frozen reference, trainable low-rank adapters and separate prompt identities for selection and evaluation. Pair responses contain real token sequences, so the optimizer evaluates chosen and rejected prefixes rather than fabricated sequence scores. The exported artifact includes every component required for offline reload. Generated preferences make optimizer and ownership failures reproducible; they do not establish natural-language ability or human alignment.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
base = torch.nn.Linear(6, 3)
a = torch.zeros(2, 6)
b = torch.zeros(3, 2)
print((base.weight + b @ a).shape)
```

## Review the evidence

Audit response masks, reference identity, adapter ownership and held-out prompt groups. Review reward/preference provenance and length effects separately before extending this controlled experiment to a real pretrained language model.
lessons.task: Implement the full synthetic preference experiment with the supplied local conditional token model and data helpers. First supervised-train the local base only on training chosen responses, freeze it as the reference, clone it and train only the two rank-two adapter matrices with response-token DPO at beta=.5. Select by validation preference loss, evaluate separate prompt identities, and export a real serialized model/reference/initialization artifact. Report actual loss, preference wins, reference-to-policy KL, parameter ownership, frozen-base hashes and reload equality. Preserve the reference report schema and prevent test preferences from fitting or selecting weights. The base is locally trained on generated pairs, not a downloaded pretrained LLM.

lessons.title: Project: train sparse experts and audit capacity under load
lessons.body:
# Project: train sparse experts and audit capacity under load

A functioning mixture-of-experts model needs routing, optimization, evaluation and overflow evidence together. This project trains a sparse classifier on generated nonlinear regions, then selects a checkpoint without seeing test targets. A separate capacity stress run reveals how admission order and dropped assignments affect the result. Export and fresh reload check that the router and every expert belong to the artifact. The experiment measures local correctness and utilization; it does not infer sparse hardware efficiency from the model’s name.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
requested = torch.tensor([0, 1, 0, 2])
print(torch.bincount(requested, minlength=4))
```

## Review the evidence

Compare quality with a dense baseline on representative data, inspect requested and accepted loads, and measure real deployment latency. Capacity-dependent predictions also require a declared batching and ordering policy.
lessons.task: Complete the generated XOR-region experiment with a four-expert, top-two sparse classifier. Train router and expert parameters with cross entropy plus .03 times the declared load-balancing auxiliary; choose only by validation cross entropy. Export model/initialization states, reload into a fresh model and evaluate held-out row identities. Report measured accuracy, load distribution, dropped assignments and a separate bounded-capacity stress run. Preserve the reference schema and keep test targets out of training/selection. Actual selected expert rows execute on CPU; this is not a GPU/distributed throughput benchmark. The CLI saves a real model and JSON report.

checks.code:

assert r['train']['loss'] < r['initial_train']['loss'] and (not torch.equal(a['state']['router.weight'], a['initial']['router.weight'])), 'Contract failed: actual router and expert training reduce the local objective.'
assert any((not torch.equal(v, a['initial'][k]) for k, v in a['state'].items() if k.startswith('experts.'))) and len(r['history']) >= 3, 'Contract failed: actual router and expert training reduce the local objective.'

checks.name: capacity stress conserves every requested assignment

assert r['test']['dropped_assignments'] == 0 and sum(r['test']['accepted_loads']) == 2 * n, 'Contract failed: capacity stress conserves every requested assignment.'
